name: Water-assisted liposuction (BodyJet)

lead: Water-assisted liposuction uses a jet of fluid to loosen fat while it is suctioned out, for a leaner body contour. BodyJet is a branded system. It is also used to collect fat for transfer to other areas such as the breast.

A fan-shaped water jet through the cannula delivers fluid and anesthetic and detaches fat, which is then aspirated. Published research is concentrated in fat-grafting and tissue-quality studies, such as case series and lab comparisons, rather than in contouring outcomes.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done by a surgeon, usually with compression garments afterwards and a recovery of several weeks. The contour change shows once swelling settles.
Risks are those of liposuction generally, including pain, bruising, contour irregularity, infection, bleeding, clots and rare deaths. No device-specific safety data were identified.

angle.text: Water-assisted liposuction, including the BodyJet system, is used for fat removal and body contouring. A water jet loosens fat before it is aspirated, and the leaner contour shows after healing. Research is mainly on fat harvesting.

lead: Water-assisted liposuction (WAL), also called water-jet-assisted liposuction, is a liposuction technique in which a fan-shaped jet of fluid is delivered through the cannula to loosen fat and infiltrate anesthetic while the fat is aspirated. BodyJet is a commercial system for the method.[1][2]

People have it to remove localized fat deposits and sharpen body contours, for example on the abdomen, flanks or thighs, so the silhouette looks leaner and more defined. The same gentle harvesting is used to collect fat that is then grafted to the breasts or other areas, adding volume where a person wants it.[3][4][5]

A 2007 randomized trial of 60 patients found much less postoperative pain with power water-assisted liposuction than with traditional tumescent liposuction, and a 2022 review describes WAL as saving time and effort for the surgeon but with lower cost performance.[6][1] Published research on the method is concentrated in fat-grafting and tissue-quality studies, with comparatively few contouring-outcome trials.[3][4][5][7]

paras: Wikipedia lists water-jet-assisted liposuction among the main liposuction variants, describing a fan-shaped water jet that delivers anesthetic and assists fat removal, with BodyJet as an example, and notes that it is commonly used for lymph-sparing lipedema surgery.[2] A 2022 Chinese review divides liposuction methods into those that separate fat by physical cutting (suction-assisted, power-assisted and water-assisted) and those that use energy (ultrasound, laser, radiofrequency); it describes SAL and PAL as simple and low-priced but dependent on surgeon experience, with uneven appearance, hematoma and ecchymosis as possible complications, and WAL as saving time and effort at lower cost performance.[1]

Wikipedia lists the main variants: tumescent (large volumes of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine to swell and numb tissue), suction-assisted, micro-cannula, power-assisted (a vibrating cannula that removes more fat with less surgeon effort and is used for difficult, scarred or large-volume areas), ultrasound-assisted, laser-assisted, radiofrequency-assisted and water-jet-assisted liposuction.[2] The ultrasound and laser variants add energy, and laser and radiofrequency approaches are described as also tightening skin, whereas the water-jet method separates fat without added heat.[2][1]

Wikipedia says liposuction is believed to work best for people of normal weight with good skin elasticity, may be done under general, regional or local anesthesia, and that small-volume procedures under about 1,000 cc can be performed awake while volumes over 5,000 cc generally need anesthesia and a hospital stay.[2] Swelling can last weeks or months after surgery.[2]

Modern liposuction began in the mid-1970s in Rome, where Arpad and Giorgio Fischer developed a blunt cannula attached to suction; Yves-Gerard Illouz extended it to the whole body and developed a wet method, and in the 1980s Jeffrey Klein published the tumescent method using large volumes of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine.[2] Water-jet assistance is a later variant. German surgeons developed the BEAULI (Berlin autologous lipotransplantation) fat-harvesting method in 2007, using BodyJet water-assisted liposuction from Humanmed AG, and evaluated it in a prospective study of 85 patients across two German centres and 216 treated breasts.[3] In 2015 liposuction became the most commonly performed cosmetic procedure in the US, according to Wikipedia.[2] Wikipedia traces the lineage further back: early body-contouring fat removal by the French surgeon Charles Dujarier, a 1926 case that set the field back for decades, European fat-cutting techniques in the late 1960s, and the Fischers' 1977 review of 245 cases in which they named the method liposculpture; Illouz later introduced the wet technique with saline and hyaluronidase.[2] A high-definition technique for accentuating abdominal muscle contours was first described in 1993.[2]

The 2010 BEAULI report describes harvesting very small fat particles with BodyJet water-assisted liposuction and reinjecting them after separating excess water, for patients with lack of breast volume, either genuine or acquired after surgery.[3] A later series of 96 breast augmentations with the BEAULI technique was published in 2013.[4]

A 2017 case series of 12 breast reconstructions used fat grafting performed with either the Coleman technique or the BodyJet system.[5] A 2017 comparison of four commercial lipotransfer protocols examined how processed fat behaved in an animal model.[7] A 2021 series of ten tuberous-breast corrections used fasciotomies and fat grafting by the BodyJet technique and assessed outcomes with BREAST-Q surveys, noting that other evidence reports higher satisfaction after implants than lipofilling.[8] A 2024 retrospective breast-centre review of 263 lipofilling treatments in 121 patients reported no major complications and one injection-site infection.[9]

A 2024 meta-analysis of liposuction techniques for lipedema included ten articles (2542 procedures in 906 patients) covering traditional tumescent, power-assisted and water-jet-assisted liposuction, and reported significant improvements in pain, bruising, swelling, pressure sensitivity and cosmetic impairment across techniques.[10] A 2025 retrospective series of seven patients used WAL to aspirate polyacrylamide hydrogel and remove the fibrotic capsule after breast augmentation with PAAG injections, with no postoperative complications during follow-up.[11]

Risks are those of liposuction in general. Wikipedia cites a 2015 study of 4,534 patients with complications in 1.5 percent, deaths of about 1 in 10,000 as of 2011, and serious complications including deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation, bleeding and infection; other effects include pain, bruising, seroma, numbness and contour deformities in about 20 percent of patients.[2] Wikipedia also states that liposuction is not effective for weight loss and that benefits are generally short-term in terms of overall body fat.[2] No device-specific safety data for BodyJet beyond the studies above were identified.

Wikipedia reports that removed fat cells are permanently gone but that overall body fat generally returns to pre-treatment levels within a few months, partly to the treated area but mostly to the abdomen, with visceral fat increasing, and that liposuction does not improve obesity-related metabolic disorders such as insulin resistance; volumes above 100 ml per unit of BMI were linked to higher complication risk, and the American Society of Plastic Surgeons published a 17-page safety advisory in 2009.[2] Wikipedia also records that 93 US citizens died after cosmetic surgery in the Dominican Republic between 2009 and 2022, about 90 percent of autopsy-confirmed deaths from embolism.[2]

Evidence is mainly surgical case series and laboratory comparisons. A 2007 prospective randomized trial in patients with BMI 25 to 30 and excessive localized fat compared power water-assisted liposuction with the traditional tumescent technique in 60 patients (32 versus 28); after four days 87 percent of the water-assisted group were completely pain free versus 3.6 percent of the traditional group, and ecchymosis was significantly less, and the authors concluded it produced less tissue trauma.[6] A 2015 study found that mesenchymal stem cells isolated after manual or water-jet-assisted liposuction displayed similar properties.[12] The breast fat-grafting series and lipedema meta-analysis are summarised above.[3][4][5][10] No large randomized trials of contouring outcomes specific to BodyJet were identified.

timeline.event: Fischer and colleagues in Rome develop blunt-cannula suction lipectomy; Illouz extends it.[2]
Fischer brothers review 245 cases and name the method liposculpture.[2]
German surgeons develop the BEAULI water-jet fat-harvesting method.[3]

Liposuction becomes the most commonly performed US cosmetic procedure.[2]
